blocks.content: Have you ever called a constructor with ten parameters… and had no idea what half of them meant?
new Pizza("Large", "Thin", true, false, true, false, true);

code.content: new Pizza("Large", "Thin", true, false, true, false, true);

codes.java: new Pizza("Large", "Thin", true, false, true, false, true);
codes.python: new Pizza("Large", "Thin", true, false, true, false, true);
codes.cpp: Pizza("Large", "Thin", true, false, true, false, true);
codes.javascript: new Pizza("Large", "Thin", true, false, true, false, true);

blocks.content: What does true, false, true even mean here? Nobody knows.
This is the problem the Builder Pattern solves.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245774924-1adcca22.png

new Pizza.Builder()
    .size("Large")
    .crust("Thin")
    .cheese(true)
    .pepperoni(true)
    .build();
Clean. Readable. Hard to get wrong.

The Builder Pattern is especially useful when objects have many optional fields, when constructors are getting out of hand, or when an object needs to be assembled in a specific order before it is ready to use.
Let's walk through a real example and see exactly how it works.
1. The Problem: Building a Pizza Order
blocks.text: 1. The Problem: Building a Pizza Order

blocks.content: Imagine you are building a food ordering app. A pizza order can have:
["Size (required)","Crust type (required)","Cheese (optional)","Pepperoni (optional)","Mushrooms (optional)","Extra sauce (optional)"]
The Naive Approach: Telescoping Constructors

codes.python:
class Pizza:
    def __init__(self, size, crust, cheese=False, pepperoni=False, mushrooms=False, extra_sauce=False):
        self.size = size
        self.crust = crust
        self.cheese = cheese
        self.pepperoni = pepperoni
        self.mushrooms = mushrooms
        self.extra_sauce = extra_sauce


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # What does True, False, True, False even mean?
    p1 = Pizza("Large", "Thin", True, False, True, False)
    print("Pizza created with the confusing positional-argument constructor.")

blocks.content: Using it looks like this:
What's Wrong With This?
1. Impossible to Read true, false, true, false means nothing without reading the constructor signature. Every caller has to go back and count parameters.
2. Easy to Make Mistakes Swap two booleans and you silently get the wrong pizza. No error. No warning. Just a wrong order.
3. Inflexible Want extra sauce but nothing else? You still have to pass false for every field before it. The order is fixed and non-negotiable.
4. Hard to Grow Add a new topping like jalapeños and every single constructor needs updating. Every existing caller might break.
This is exactly the problem the Builder Pattern was designed to fix.
2. What is the Builder Pattern?
The Builder Pattern separates the construction of a complex object from its representation letting you build the same type of object in many different configurations, cleanly and safely.
Two ideas define it:
1. Step-by-step construction instead of passing everything to a constructor at once, you set each field through individual method calls. You only call the methods for the fields you actually need.
2. Fluent interface each method returns the builder itself, so you can chain calls into one clean, readable expression that ends with build().
Before: Telescoping Constructor
Pizza pizza = new Pizza("Large", "Thin", true, false, true, false);

code.content: Pizza pizza = new Pizza("Large", "Thin", true, false, true, false);

codes.java: Pizza pizza = new Pizza("Large", "Thin", true, false, true, false);
codes.python: Pizza pizza = new Pizza("Large", "Thin", true, false, true, false);
codes.cpp: Pizza pizza("Large", "Thin", true, false, true, false);
codes.javascript: Pizza pizza = new Pizza("Large", "Thin", true, false, true, false);

blocks.content: After: Builder Pattern

Pizza pizza = new Pizza.Builder("Large", "Thin")
    .cheese(true)
    .mushrooms(true)
    .build();
Instantly clear. Only the fields you need nothing else.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245775060-f4b6f860.png
The Builder Pattern involves four participants:
Client initiates the building process. Either works directly with the builder through fluent chaining, or delegates to a Director for standard configurations.
Director (Optional) knows the steps to build common configurations like a Margherita or BBQ Chicken pizza. Calls builder methods in the right order so the client doesn't have to.
Builder exposes methods to configure the product step by step. Each method returns the builder itself to enable fluent chaining.
ConcreteBuilder implements the builder, stores intermediate state, and implements build() to validate inputs and produce the final object.
Product the final object being constructed. Often immutable with a private constructor that accepts the builder.
3. How It Works
The Builder workflow follows a simple four-step process:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245775349-f52c1b66.png
Step 1: Create the Builder The client creates a Builder and passes any required fields like size and crust to its constructor.

Step 2: Configure Optional Fields The client calls methods on the Builder for each optional field it needs. Every method returns the Builder itself enabling clean chaining. The order of calls does not matter.
Step 3: Build the Product The client calls build(). The Builder validates all fields and passes itself to the Pizza's private constructor, which copies the configured state into immutable fields.
Step 4: Use the Product The client receives a fully constructed, immutable Pizza. The Builder can be discarded or reused to create a different configuration.
4. Implementing Builder
Let's implement the Builder Pattern for our Pizza example. We create the Product class with a private constructor and a static nested Builder class.
1. Create the Product (Pizza) and Builder

We start by creating the Pizza class the product we want to build. Required fields go into the Builder's constructor. Optional fields have sensible defaults. The Pizza constructor is private, forcing clients to use the Builder.
2. Using the Builder from Client Code
blocks.text: 2. Using the Builder from Client Code

blocks.content: Here is how clients order different types of pizzas:

codes.python:
class Pizza:
    def __init__(self, builder):
        self.size = builder.size
        self.crust = builder.crust
        self.cheese = builder.cheese
        self.pepperoni = builder.pepperoni
        self.mushrooms = builder.mushrooms
        self.extra_sauce = builder.extra_sauce

    def __str__(self):
        return (f"Pizza{{size='{self.size}', crust='{self.crust}', "
                f"cheese={str(self.cheese).lower()}, pepperoni={str(self.pepperoni).lower()}, "
                f"mushrooms={str(self.mushrooms).lower()}, extraSauce={str(self.extra_sauce).lower()}}}")

    class Builder:
        def __init__(self, size, crust):
            self.size = size
            self.crust = crust
            self.cheese = False
            self.pepperoni = False
            self.mushrooms = False
            self.extra_sauce = False

        def set_cheese(self, cheese):
            self.cheese = cheese
            return self

        def set_pepperoni(self, pepperoni):
            self.pepperoni = pepperoni
            return self

        def set_mushrooms(self, mushrooms):
            self.mushrooms = mushrooms
            return self

        def set_extra_sauce(self, extra_sauce):
            self.extra_sauce = extra_sauce
            return self

        def build(self):
            return Pizza(self)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Plain pizza, just size and crust
    plain = Pizza.Builder("Small", "Thin").build()

    # Cheese and pepperoni only
    classic = Pizza.Builder("Large", "Thick").set_cheese(True).set_pepperoni(True).build()

    # Fully loaded pizza
    loaded = (Pizza.Builder("Large", "Stuffed")
              .set_cheese(True)
              .set_pepperoni(True)
              .set_mushrooms(True)
              .set_extra_sauce(True)
              .build())

    print(plain)
    print(classic)
    print(loaded)

blocks.content: Compare this to the telescoping constructor version. Every field is named. No confusingtrue, false, true, false. No positional guessing. You set only what you need in any order you want.
What We Achieved

["No telescoping constructors. Each field is set by name through a dedicated method no null arguments, no positional confusion.","Readable and self-documenting. The chain of method calls reads like a natural description of the pizza being ordered.","Immutable product. Once built, the Pizza cannot be modified. Safe to share across threads.","Easy to extend. Adding a new topping means adding one method to the Builder. No existing code breaks.","Flexible ordering. Call builder methods in any order. No positional coupling whatsoever."]
items: No telescoping constructors. Each field is set by name through a dedicated method no null arguments, no positional confusion.
Readable and self-documenting. The chain of method calls reads like a natural description of the pizza being ordered.
Immutable product. Once built, the Pizza cannot be modified. Safe to share across threads.
Easy to extend. Adding a new topping means adding one method to the Builder. No existing code breaks.
Flexible ordering. Call builder methods in any order. No positional coupling whatsoever.

blocks.content: 5. The Director Pattern
So far, the client has been calling builder methods directly. But what happens when multiple parts of your app need to order the same type of pizza?
For example, every Monday special needs the same toppings, size, and crust. Duplicating that configuration across 20 order points is a maintenance problem waiting to happen.
The Director solves this by encapsulating common construction sequences into named methods. Instead of every client knowing how to configure a builder, the Director provides pre-built recipes.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245775541-c82ddae7.png
Director Implementation
Output:
When to Use a Director
The Director is optional and in many codebases you will not need one. Here is when each approach makes sense:
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245775812-80c45841.jpg
hink of the Director as a menu of pre-built recipes. If you find yourself copying the same builder chain in three places, that is a signal to introduce a Director.
6. Practical Example: Email Builder
A real-world email builder that constructs email messages step by step. This is a common pattern in email libraries and notification systems.

codes.python:
class Email: def __init__(self, builder): self.from_ = builder.from_ self.to = list(builder.to) self.cc = list(builder.cc) self.subject = builder.subject self.body = builder.body self.is_html = builder.is_html self.reply_to = builder.reply_to def send(self): print("-----------------------------") print(f"FROM : {self.from_}") print(f"TO : {', '.join(self.to)}") if self.cc: print(f"CC : {', '.join(self.cc)}") if self.reply_to is not None: print(f"REPLY-TO: {self.reply_to}") print(f"SUBJECT : {self.subject}") print(f"FORMAT : {'HTML' if self.is_html else 'Plain Text'}") print(f"BODY : {self.body}") print("-----------------------------") print("Email sent successfully!") class Builder: def __init__(self, from_, subject): self.from_ = from_ self.subject = subject self.to = [] self.cc = [] self.body = "" self.is_html = False self.reply_to = None def set_to(self, *recipients): self.to.extend(recipients) return self def set_cc(self, *recipients): self.cc.extend(recipients) return self def set_body(self, body): self.body = body return self def html_body(self, body): self.body = body self.is_html = True return self def set_reply_to(self, reply_to): self.reply_to = reply_to return self def build(self): if not self.to: raise ValueError("Email must have at least one recipient.") return Email(self) if __name__ == "__main__": # Simple plain text email welcome = (Email.Builder("no-reply@app.com", "Welcome to the Platform!") .set_to("alice@example.com") .set_body("Hi Alice, thanks for signing up!") .build()) # HTML email with CC and reply-to invoice = (Email.Builder("billing@app.com", "Your Invoice for October") .set_to("bob@example.com") .set_cc("accounts@app.com", "manager@app.com") .html_body("
